reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease / restrictive cardiomyopathy literature
clinicalPearls: A major cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy in tropical and subtropical regions, especially equatorial Africa
Dense fibrosis of the ventricular endocardium and inflow tracts restricts filling and distorts the valves
Right-sided disease causes prominent ascites, raised venous pressure, and hepatomegaly, sometimes out of proportion to peripheral oedema
Left-sided disease produces pulmonary congestion and mitral regurgitation from fibrosis of the subvalvular apparatus
Apical obliteration by fibrosis and thrombus is characteristic on imaging
It sits within the hypereosinophilic spectrum, and Loffler endocarditis is regarded as an earlier active phase
Management is largely supportive, with surgical endocardial resection and valve repair in selected advanced cases
reference.pathophysiology: Endomyocardial fibrosis is characterised by progressive fibrous thickening of the endocardium of one or both ventricular apices and inflow regions. It is widely linked to the toxic effects of eosinophil granule proteins, so that an initial eosinophilic and inflammatory phase, exemplified by Loffler endocarditis, evolves into a burnt-out fibrotic stage. The rigid fibrotic endocardium and overlying mural thrombus obliterate the ventricular apices, impair diastolic filling to produce restrictive physiology, and tether the atrioventricular valves, causing regurgitation and progressive heart failure.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiac amyloidosis and other infiltrative cardiomyopathies
Loffler endocarditis in its active eosinophilic phase
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography showing apical obliteration, endocardial thickening, and atrioventricular valve involvement
Cardiac MRI to characterise fibrosis and thrombus with late enhancement
Full blood count and eosinophil assessment to identify a hypereosinophilic driver
ECG demonstrating conduction and repolarisation abnormalities
Cardiac catheterisation showing restrictive filling and, when needed, endomyocardial biopsy
redFlags: Progressive heart failure with intractable ascites
Systemic embolism from apical mural thrombus
reference.prognosis: Advanced endomyocardial fibrosis carries a poor prognosis with progressive heart failure, and outcomes in the fibrotic stage are limited; surgery may improve symptoms in selected patients but operative risk is significant.
pitfalls: Confusing it with constrictive pericarditis, which is surgically curable
Missing an underlying hypereosinophilic disorder in the active phase
Overlooking apical thrombus and the resulting embolic risk
Attributing isolated right-sided features to primary liver disease
management: In the early active eosinophilic (Loffler) phase, treat the hypereosinophilia with corticosteroids and, where indicated, further cytoreductive or targeted therapy to limit progression to fibrosis
Manage the resulting restrictive heart failure with diuretics for congestion and control of atrial arrhythmia
Give anticoagulation for mural thrombus and to reduce thromboembolic risk
Consider surgical endocardial decortication with atrioventricular valve repair or replacement in selected advanced cases to relieve restriction
Monitor disease activity and complications with serial echocardiography and eosinophil counts
Manage conduction disease and arrhythmia, considering device therapy where indicated
Refer to cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, and evaluate advanced or refractory disease for transplantation
